query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The coupled response of high-entropy alloys to tribo-corrosion is governed by the formation of a stable, dense oxide layer on the surface, which prevents further oxidation and reduces wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a specific composition and microstructure
generation.intervention: Tribo-corrosion testing in a controlled environment
generation.conditions: Variation of temperature, humidity, and mechanical stress
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable, dense oxide layer on the surface
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxidation and reduces wear and corrosion by preventing the penetration of corrosive species and reducing the coefficient of friction
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced wear and corrosion rates, improved mechanical properties, and enhanced thermal stability
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with no oxide layer
generation.boundary: Limitations of the oxide layer's stability and density, as well as the alloy's composition and microstructure
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms by which the oxide layer forms and interacts with the alloy's microstructure, as well as the effects of varying environmental conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled tribo-corrosion testing of high-entropy alloys with varying oxide layer formation and density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide layer is found to have no significant effect on wear and corrosion rates, or if the alloy's composition and microstructure are found to have a dominant effect on the coupled response, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications (e.g. fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. At the same time, in several works [,,], it was shown that the variation of the components of high-entropy alloys leads to a change in the resistance to radiation-induced swelling and subsequent embrittlement and in some cases, an increase in structural stability in comparison with classical nuclear materials subjected to similar radiation exposure. The increased stability is primarily due to the fact that when varying the alloy components, additional grain boundaries are created, as well as, in some cases, the formation of a high density of dislocations and vacancy defects, the presence of which causes the effects of inhibition of the ability to agglomerate implanted ions in the near-surface layer [,]. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a kind of novel materials known for their exceptional mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability , , . Noting that HEAs have high mixing-entropy, it is expected to form face-centered cubic (FCC), body-centered cubic (BCC), and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases , . Researchers are increasingly focuses on the application of HEAs in the conditions of CE, driven by the aforementioned outstanding performances. For example, Zhang et al.  documented that the AlCrCoFeNi HEA demonstrated superior CE resistance and higher pitting corrosion resistance compared to 304L SS. Nair et al.  conducted a study revealing that the Al0.1CoCrFeNi HEA exhibited a notably longer CE incubation period and a reduced corrosion rate (approximately one-fourth) compared to 316L SS. Additionally, Wu et al.  discovered that the hardness of FeCoCrAlNiTi2 HEA was at least 3.6 times that of 304 SS, and demonstrate excellent CE resistance. These studies indicate that HEAs may have the prospects to be successfully used in the field of CE.

For HEAs to reach their full potential, it is essential to predict the phases that ultimately form. Wang et al. studied the microstructure and mechanical properties of as-cast and as-annealed CoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloys and found that a high strain hardening rate is observed due to the high density of dislocation tangles surrounding the μ-phase precipitates, resulting in significant strength improvement. Stepanov et al. studied the effect of vanadium content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the CoCrFeMnNiVx high-entropy alloys and found that V content in the alloy system results in the emergence and growth of the σ phase, which results in a noticeable drop in ductility. To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are different from traditional alloys, which are composed of multiple principal elements. Due to the high entropy effect, slow diffusion effect, lattice distortion, and cocktail effect [], HEAs have unique and excellent characteristics, such as high strength [,], excellent oxidation resistance at elevated temperature [,], and good wear resistance [,], which have received extensive attention from domestic and foreign scholars. CoCrFeMnNi HEA shows excellent mechanical properties due to the forming a single FCC phase, with excellent elongation of 60–70%, tensile strength of more than 1 GPa, fracture toughness of more than 200 GPa, and excellent damage resistance []. Therefore, CoCrFeMnNi HEA is an essential candidate for new materials of critical components in industrial applications, such as die manufacturing, aerospace, defense-heavy industry, and nuclear industry [,,,]. In these practical industrial applications, friction and wear behavior is essential. These key components and parts need well mechanical properties and outstanding wear resistance [,,].
